title: Insufficient Jurisdictional Evidence
question: What Utah regulation currently adopts the FDA Food Code 2026, and what penalties does it impose on a restaurant that violates employee-illness rules?
final_result: Insufficient evidence: The question asks for (1) a specific current Utah regulation that adopts the FDA Food Code 2026 and (2) the penalties that Utah law imposes on a restaurant violating employee-illness rules. Nothing in the retrieved collection supports either part. The only Utah document available (Utah Risk Factor Study, 2016-2017) is a historical analysis of local retail food inspection line-item violations; it states only that the Utah Department of Health "oversees and administers rules and policies that provide regulatory standards of operation for food safety and authority for local health departments to enforce those standards," without naming any rule, its adoption of any Food Code edition, or any penalty amounts. The FDA Food Code 2026 is a model code that becomes binding only where a jurisdiction separately adopts it; its Annex 7 model ordinance uses blank placeholders such as "(name of adopting authority)" and "(name of jurisdiction)" and its examples of fines/sentences cover only California, Maryland, Texas, and federal law (no Utah). Food Code 8-911.10 leaves the fine amount to be designated by the adopting jurisdiction ("A fine of not more than (designate amount) dollars"), and 8-501.20 provides only non-monetary control measures (restriction, exclusion, or summary permit suspension/closure) as examples of enforcement, not Utah penalties. Because the central request — the Utah adopting rule and its penalty amounts — is absent, no answer can be given from these sources.

Foodborne illnesses continue to be a public health concern in Utah. Utah’s local health
departments are responsible to inspect food service businesses in Utah and to respond to foodborne
illness complaints or outbreaks. The Utah Department of Health (UDOH) provides training and support
to the local health departments. In addition, UDOH oversees and administers rules and policies that
provide regulatory standards of operation for food safety and authority for local health departments to
enforce those standards. The UDOH conducted an analysis of data from retail food inspections
conducted in 2016 by local inspectors. This analysis was done through a cooperative agreement with
the Association of Food and Drug Officials (AFDO) administering a grant from the U.S. Food and Drug
Administration (FDA).

Purpose:
The purpose of this analysis is to evaluate trends, patterns, and correlations of food code
violations with the intent of finding ways of improving the efficacy and efficiency of food establishment
inspections by local departments, and to identify priorities for focused training and policy development
by UDOH.
